name: Calibration and conformal prediction for histogram / classification-as-regression outputs: temperature scaling (Guo 2017), quantile/isotonic recalibration (Kuleshov 2018), distribution calibration (Song 2019), conformal histogram regression CHR (Sesia & Romano 2021), probabilistic/multimodal conformal PCP (Wang et al. 2023), conformal prediction under HMMs and dependent data (2022-2024), plus an empirical calibration audit of Erudition's 155-well holdout posteriors

Song et al. ICML 2019, PMLR 97:5897-5906 (https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/song19a.html). code_availability: CHR: github.com/msesia/chr (Python). Temperature scaling / isotonic: a few lines (sklearn IsotonicRegression). Kuleshov tutorial: github.com/AnthonyRentsch/calibrated_regression. Audit scripts for our posteriors: scratchpad calib.py / modecal.py (numpy only, reproducible on posterior_all.npz); not committed.
evidence_level: Peer-reviewed methods (ICML/NeurIPS). Our own audit on 155 holdout wells (23,634 columns, 60-epoch baseline dump) is a direct measurement; out-of-sample recalibration numbers use 2-fold well-grouped CV within the holdout set (fitting on training wells would be the proper protocol).
extreme_summary: Post-hoc calibration (temperature, isotonic/quantile, mode-mass Platt) and conformal wrappers (CHR, PCP, well-level split conformal) can make histogram posteriors reliable and give coverage-guaranteed intervals, but for pooled RMSE under the mean decode they only help if the posterior mean is mis-calibrated. Our audit shows the 60-epoch ConvNeXt posterior is already mean- and variance-calibrated (slope of truth on mean 0.993, predicted variance 30.5 vs actual MSE 29.9 ft^2, NLL minimal at T=1.0): temperature scaling does not help out of sample (5.52 vs 5.47 ft) and CV mode-mass recalibration gains 0.017 ft, far below the 0.39 ft noise floor. The useful product is per-well confidence: posterior spread ranks well RMSE with Spearman 0.64 and well-level split conformal gives valid 90% coverage.
task_definition: Given a model's predictive distribution p(y|x) (here a 400-bin histogram over TVT per MD column), (a) recalibrate it so that probabilities match frequencies, and/or (b) produce prediction sets with finite-sample coverage guarantees; downstream (c) flag low-confidence wells.
inputs: Model posterior histograms (our per-column 400-bin softmax), a held-out calibration set of wells with truth, optionally per-well covariates (entropy, number of significant modes, well length).
target_parameterisation: Unchanged (TVT offset per column). Calibration acts on the output distribution only.
output_representation: Recalibrated per-column histogram; conformal interval or union of intervals (CHR gives shortest interval from the histogram; PCP gives unions of balls, i.e. multimodal sets); per-well predicted RMSE with conformal upper bound.
architecture: Post-hoc, no network change. Temperature: p_T proportional to p^(1/T), one scalar. Isotonic/quantile recalibration (Kuleshov): monotone map on the predicted CDF value (PIT) fitted on calibration data. Distribution calibration (Song): GP with Beta link mapping predicted to calibrated distributions. Mode-mass calibration (our variant): per-column basins from posterior_analysis.find_modes, dominant-mode mass recalibrated by Platt a*logit+b, other modes rescaled. CHR: nested histogram-based intervals conformalised on a calibration set. PCP: sample K points from the predictive, the set is a union of balls with conformal radius. HMM/dependent conformal: exchangeability restored at the level of blocks/chains or via online adaptive conformal with particle-filter states.
core_mechanism: Under pooled squared loss the Bayes decode is the posterior mean, and RMSE depends on the posterior only through its mean. So calibration lowers RMSE exactly when E[y | mu_hat] != mu_hat, e.g. systematic over/under-confidence of dominant band weights that biases the mean toward the wrong band. Temperature and isotonic maps change the mean only by reshaping multimodal columns (moving weight between humps); for unimodal symmetric columns they change intervals but not the mean. Conformal methods guarantee marginal coverage under exchangeability (valid across wells if wells are exchangeable) but do not change the point prediction.
training_objective: Post-hoc: NLL (temperature), isotonic least squares on PIT (Kuleshov), GP marginal likelihood (Song), or directly the SSE of the recalibrated mean (what matters for us; our mode-mass Platt fit minimised SSE). Conformal: quantile of nonconformity scores on the calibration set; no training. In-training alternatives (not reviewed in depth): label smoothing, focal loss, mixup; our targets are already smoothed (alignment_exp_smooth_sigma 1.25).
decoding: Keep the expectation of the recalibrated histogram (RMSE-consistent). Conformal sets are for reporting/flagging, not for the point estimate.
metric_consistent_decode: Yes if the expectation of the (re)calibrated posterior is used. Anything that uses calibration to justify picking the dominant mode is mode-seeking and raised RMSE in our repo (argmax 6.26, dominant mode 6.06 vs mean 5.47 ft).
evidence_scope: Per column (temperature, isotonic, mode mass); per well for conformal flags (well-level exchangeability).
prefix_conditioning: Not intrinsic. A per-well temperature fitted on the known heel prefix would be a test-time calibration (B10 territory) but the prefix posterior is conditioned on known labels and not representative of the suffix.
propose_vs_select: Neither; it reweights an existing posterior. Can calibrate the inputs of a gate or blend (calibrated posteriors blend better).
dataset: Literature: UCI regression, time series, CIFAR/ImageNet (temperature), synthetic/skewed regression (CHR). Our audit: 155 holdout wells, 23,634 MD columns (32 rows each), posterior_all.npz from the 60-epoch ConvNeXt baseline (seq_NN_posterior_dump.py --save-all).
synthetic_to_real: Relevant: 85% synthetic training could miscalibrate real-well posteriors, but the audit on real holdout wells shows no material miscalibration of mean or variance, so the synthetic mix has not produced a systematic confidence bias at the 60-epoch checkpoint.
metric_and_performance: Audit on 155 holdout wells (column-level pooled RMSE, mean decode 5.469 ft): (1) mean calibration: weighted regression truth = -0.19 + 0.993 * mu. (2) Variance: mean predicted variance 30.5 ft^2 vs actual MSE 29.9 ft^2; z-score std 1.17 (heavy tails). (3) Shape: PIT deciles 0.078/0.060/0.061/0.074/0.101/0.128/0.143/0.136/0.112/0.106; central 50% interval covers 64% (core too wide), 80% covers 84%, 90% covers 90.3%, 95% covers 93.8% (tails too thin), mean 90% width 13.2 ft. (4) Temperature (in-sample): T=0.8/0.9/1.0/1.1/1.25 give RMSE 5.472/5.466/5.469/5.479/5.506 and NLL minimum at T=1.0; well-grouped 2-fold CV temperature (fit on SSE) 5.517 +- 0.049 ft, i.e. worse. (5) Mode-mass reliability (3,730 multimodal columns): dominant-mass bins 0.55/0.65/0.75/0.86/0.93 have truth-under-dominant rates 0.59/0.70/0.81/0.76/0.85 (roughly calibrated, slightly over-confident above 0.8). CV Platt recalibration of mode masses (sharpening, a~1.4-1.6): 5.463 vs 5.480 ft (unweighted column RMSE), gain 0.017 ft; in-sample optimum 5.452 ft. (6) Per-well confidence: Spearman(posterior sd, actual well RMSE) = 0.64 (p=5e-19); the 10 wells with the largest predicted sd hold 33% of well-level SSE (oracle top-10: 46%); well-level split conformal on ratio actual RMSE / predicted sd, 90% level: empirical coverage 0.91 over 200 random 77/78 splits, threshold ratio 1.65 (median ratio 0.73). Literature: CHR attains nominal coverage with shorter intervals than CQR on skewed data; Kuleshov recalibration gives calibrated intervals and improves forecasting/RL downstream.
comparability: The audit is directly comparable (same 155 holdout wells, same metric), with two caveats: column-level truth is the mean of 32 rows (so 5.469 vs row-level 5.474 ft), and it is the 60-epoch baseline, not the 4.84 ft FastViT or 4.69 ft blend, which should be re-audited.
validation_protocol: CV within holdout wells, grouped by well, repeated random 2-fold (20 repeats for temperature, 10 for mode-mass Platt). Proper deployment would fit calibrators on training/OOF wells and evaluate once on the holdout; with synthetic-heavy training that requires real-well OOF posteriors.
inference_budget: Negligible (one power and renormalisation per column, or a 1-D isotonic lookup; conformal is a quantile lookup).
repeated_layers: Calibration can only redistribute weight between humps that already exist; it cannot identify the correct band. The audit shows dominant-band weights are roughly calibrated, so the 51% of SSE from band confusion is irreducible by recalibration of this posterior; it needs more evidence (inputs, neighbour wells, path-level evidence) or a better model. Multimodal conformal (PCP, CHR with disjoint sets) can express 'band A or band B' as a two-piece set for reporting.
drift: Not addressed: a hump sliding away from truth is a mean error that calibration cannot correct unless it is systematic across wells (the regression intercept of -0.19 ft and slope 0.993 show it is not).
uncertainty_and_calibration: Core topic. Findings: well calibrated in mean and variance; mild shape miscalibration (under-dispersed core, heavy tails, PIT hump at deciles 5-8); per-well spread is a useful ranking signal and supports conformal flagging with valid coverage. Ensembles/blends (averaging probabilities of two models) typically become under-confident and multimodal averages shift weight, so blended posteriors need a separate audit.
where_to_use: (1) Diagnostic gate in the evaluation pipeline (new script next to posterior_analysis.py, e.g. posterior_calibration.py): run on every new posterior dump and on blends before trusting a blend weight. (2) Blend-time calibration: temperature per member before probability averaging in the pair/ensemble blend (ConvNeXt + FastViT or ConvNeXt + AnchorCNN), fitted on OOF training wells. (3) Per-well confidence flag and conformal bound for reporting / rig use (not for RMSE).
error_mode_targeted: Measurement/protocol and blend quality; marginally 'blend' (15%) and 'wrong_mode' (24%) via mode-mass reweighting, but the audit shows little recoverable error there.
gap_vs_our_implementation: Not done before: no calibration audit existed; now measured (see metric_and_performance). Confirmed not a gap for single-model RMSE: temperature and mode-mass recalibration give <= 0.02 ft out of sample on the 60-epoch baseline, and the posterior mean is essentially unbiased. Remaining gaps: (1) the audit has not been run on the deployed FastViT-SA12 distilled student (4.84 ft) or on the 4.69 ft pair; KD with a temperature can change calibration, and probability averaging of two models changes dispersion, so per-member temperature before averaging is untested. (2) No per-well confidence output: posterior sd predicts well RMSE (Spearman 0.64) and a well-level conformal bound is valid at 90%, which could flag the worst wells (the worst 10 wells carry ~48% of SSE) for fallback to a different model or for human review. (3) Heavy tails (z std 1.17, 95% interval covers 93.8%) mean interval reporting should use conformal quantiles rather than raw posterior quantiles.
proposed_experiment: E0 (done, CPU, ~2 min): calibration audit on baseline_check_posterior_all (numbers above). E1 (CPU, <1 h): rerun the audit on posterior dumps of the FastViT-SA12 student and the ConvNeXt teacher (seq_NN_posterior_dump.py --save-all for each) and on their probability average; report mean-calibration slope, var ratio, PIT, NLL-vs-T. If the average is under-confident (var ratio > 1.1 or NLL minimum at T < 0.9), E2: fit a temperature per member on training-well OOF posteriors (or 2-fold within holdout as a quick check), average tempered posteriors, decode by expectation; compare with the current blend at matched weight on the 155 wells; accept only if gain > 0.39 ft (expected gain is small; mainly a sanity check). E3 (confidence flag): compute per-well predicted RMSE = sqrt(mean posterior variance over suffix columns); fit the 90% conformal ratio threshold on training wells; on holdout report coverage, and test a routing rule 'if predicted well RMSE > q, use the other model / blend weight 0.5' with the threshold chosen on training wells only. Files: new kaggle_1st_place/solution/posterior_calibration.py (reuse posterior_analysis.softmax/level_axis and the npz loader from posterior_fb_decode.py); no training changes.
implementation_effort: Low: numpy-only post-hoc analysis; the audit script already exists in prototype form.
gpu_cost: None beyond one inference dump per model (minutes on the RTX 5060); calibration fitting is CPU-only.
distillation_compatibility: Compatible and relevant: KD temperature and teacher calibration shape the student's posterior; auditing the student and, if needed, tempering the teacher targets during KD is a zero-cost check.
error_correlation_with_ours: Not a blend member; it is a monotone transform of our own posterior and so perfectly correlated. Its value is in making blends and gates better conditioned.
risk: (1) Measured: the posterior is already calibrated, so expected RMSE gain for a single model is ~0.01-0.02 ft, well below the 0.39 ft noise floor. (2) Fitting calibrators on the holdout itself leaks; with only 618 real training wells and 85% synthetic training data, OOF real-well posteriors are needed for a clean fit. (3) Conformal validity assumes wells are exchangeable between calibration and test; spatial clustering of wells (and Kaggle private test) can break this. (4) Per-well flags only help RMSE if there is a better fallback for flagged wells; our previous learned gates failed (5.017 vs 4.905).
notes: Key conclusion for the metric: band-confusion error cannot be removed by recalibrating the current posterior; the evidence must change. This is consistent with the outline's framing and now quantified. Interesting side facts: the PIT hump at deciles 5-8 with mean z near 0 indicates a slight skew (median below mean) in typical columns; in-sample, mild sharpening (T=0.9) is optimal for RMSE while T=1.0 is optimal for NLL, but the difference (0.003 ft) is noise. The 'conformal under HMM' literature (Markov de Finetti, particle-filter ACI) matters only if intervals are produced sequentially along the lateral in real time; for offline pooled-RMSE scoring, well-level split conformal is sufficient.
